gap: No result ChatGPT got works out whether a bus-powered switch can actually power the SSD. The sum: a USB 3.x SSD can draw up to 0.9 A, and a keyboard and mouse at one USB 2.0 unit load each add 0.2 A, so the three need 1.1 A (5.5 W). The UGREEN CM691 passes on up to 2.4 A from a USB-C host, which leaves 1.3 A spare. A USB-A host port is only required to supply 0.9 A, which is 0.2 A less than the three devices need. That makes the shopper's own 'is one computer USB-A?' question a question about power, not just speed.
standout_why: I compared against the cited UGREEN product pages, digitaldesksolutions.com (2026-10-28) and our own 2026-11-03 page. digitaldesksolutions does one 1,400 mA vs 900 mA sum for a made-up webcam setup on a generic USB 3.0 switch. It doesn't name a product's power budget and doesn't treat the USB-A host case. The UGREEN page says the switch 'can output 5V2A' from a USB-A port without saying that a spec-minimum USB-A 3.x port only supplies 0.9 A. Our page gives 12 W and 9 W budgets (the 9 W rests on '1.8 A', but the store page now says 2 A) and never subtracts the devices. No page compares the SSD's draw with the host port's minimum. All of them, ours included, already give 100 GB copy times at 10 vs 5 Gbps, so that sum adds nothing new.
decides: This confirms the UGREEN CM691 ($40.99 today; the $69.99 ChatGPT showed in one chat is the store's struck-through compare-at price) as the pick when both computers have USB-C: a keyboard, mouse and USB-spec SSD leave 1.3 A (6.5 W) spare. If either computer only has USB-A, the bus-powered CM691 and ATEN US3342 can't be counted on to power the SSD, since a 0.9 A port is 0.2 A short of the 1.1 A load. ATEN in fact requires a 5 V 3 A host. For that case the page should send the shopper to a switch with its own power input: Cable Matters 201160 with its optional adapter, or UGREEN's 7-port 10Gbps model with its included adapter.

findings.label: Spare current with keyboard + mouse + SSD, USB-C host
findings.source_title: UGREEN USBC Switch - 2-Port, 4 x USB 3.2, 10Gbps Data
findings.note: Load = SSD 0.9 A (USB 3.x high-power limit) + keyboard 0.1 A + mouse 0.1 A (one USB 2.0 unit load each), from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USB_3.0 = 1.1 A. Spare: 2.4 − 1.1 = 1.3 A; 1.3 A × 5 V = 6.5 W.

findings.label: Current short on a USB-A 3.x host port at its spec minimum
findings.value: 0.2 A short (0.9 A supplied vs 1.1 A load)
findings.note: Quote: 'For high-power SuperSpeed devices, the limit is six unit loads, or 900 mA (4.5 W).' A USB-A host port is only required to supply 0.9 A, but the load is 1.1 A: 0.9 − 1.1 = −0.2 A. UGREEN's 2 A from USB-A only applies if the host port supplies more than the spec requires.

findings.label: Ceiling on a spec-compliant portable SSD's draw
findings.value: ≤0.9 A at 5 V (4.5 W) on USB 3.x
findings.note: Samsung: 'The T7 Shield complies with official USB power specifications'; interface 'USB 3.2 Gen.2 (10Gbps)', up to 1,050 MB/s read. Combined with Wikipedia's 900 mA limit this caps the drive at 4.5 W. It's an upper bound, not a measurement.
